title: Queued Backpressure Orchestrator for Dedicated Fleets
creator: Ava Chen
description: Background: Dedicated pools see bursty, mixed-priority traffic (interactive chat, async batch, embeddings) that can violate per-customer throughput guarantees and cause noisy-neighbor latency spikes. Existing admission logic either sheds broadly or enforces static per-route limits, which leads to unfair drops and expensive fallbacks. Goal: build a queued backpressure orchestrator (QBO) that enforces throughput contracts at the fleet and tenant level while minimizing user-visible latency and maximizing successful request throughput. QBO will combine: (1) lightweight per-tenant soft queues with bounded tail size; (2) token-bucket rate harmonization across levels (tenant -> route -> fleet); (3) queue coalescing and request batching hints for the autoscaler; (4) graceful drain + fallback to compatible model variants instead of outright drops. The system must support predictable throughput SLAs, signal the autoscaler with queue depth metrics, and allow operational overrides (emergency capacity and maintenance drains).
design_decisions: Use soft, in-memory FIFO queues per-tenant with two priority lanes (interactive vs background) to preserve low tail latency for interactive traffic
Implement a hierarchical token-bucket: tenant -> product-route -> fleet. Tokens can be borrowed from lower priority lanes during sustained headroom but reclaimed on pressure
Queue coalescing: collapse small concurrent requests from same tenant into a single batched execution hint when model & prompt compatibility allows
Autoscaler integration: expose queue depth percentiles and time-to-schedule metrics over a metrics endpoint and a webhook for urgent scale requests
Fallback strategy: prefer model-variant fallback with documented quality degradation path; only shed when no compatible variant or capacity exists
Operational controls: admin API to set emergency policy, drain pools, and reassign tenant weightings without deployment
implementation_plan: Spike (1 week): prototype per-tenant soft queue and token-bucket logic in a feature branch; run synthetic load to validate q-depth signals
Core (2 weeks): implement hierarchical token-bucket enforcement and borrow/reclaim logic in runtime admission path
Queue coalescing (1 week): implement batch-hint generation and compatibility checks (size, seq-len, model-variant)
Autoscaler hooks (1 week): add metrics (p50/p95 queue depth, avg wait time) and webhook to autoscaler service
Fallbacks and shedding (1 week): implement graceful model-variant fallback path and final shedding policy with observability
Integrations & testing (1 week): chaos testing (node failures, burst patterns), end-to-end load tests, and SLAs verification
Docs & rollout (ongoing): console controls, runbook updates, and customer-facing routing docs
acceptance_criteria: Fleet-level throughput contracts are met within 5% for synthetic tenant workloads across a range of burst patterns
Interactive lane p95 latency improves or stays within SLA compared to baseline under mixed load
Autoscaler receives queue-driven scale hints and responds (scale event fired) during sustained queue pressure in integration test
Fallbacks trigger for compatible model variants with clear audit logs; shedding only occurs when no compatibility/fallback exists
Admin override can set emergency capacities and drain behavior without code changes
Instrumentation: dashboard shows per-tenant queue depths, borrow/reclaim events, fallback occurrences, and shed counts
rollout_plan: Feature flag behind tenant opt-in in staging; run with a small set of internal tenants for 48h
Canary to 10% of fleets with telemetry checks for throughput and latency regressions
Progressive ramp to 50% with automated rollback triggers on p95 latency or shed spikes
Full rollout after 7 days of stable metrics and sign-off from SRE and PM
Post-rollout: runbook dry-run, customer communications for tenants that hit fallbacks
